extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy; philosophers and people interested in epistemology
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for clear philosophical inquiry about human understanding: how ideas arise, how knowledge and assent are formed, and how to avoid confusion from vague language or improper claims (e.g., innateness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determined ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: When applied to a complex idea, one should mean such an one as consists of a determinate number of certain simple or less complex ideas, joined in such a proportion and situation as the mind has before its view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer 'determined ideas' to indeterminate ones: have a precise, determinate idea in mind that a name stands for and keep that idea steadily annexed to the name during the present discourse. Locke argues this reduces mistakes and ends many doubts and disputes that depend on doubtful or uncertain use of words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use a word without its precise idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid using any word until you view in your mind the precise determined idea which you resolve to make it the sign of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antipattern: casual or shifting use of terms. If a speaker/writer uses a term without a stable idea in mind, expect obscurity and confusion in thought and discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define terms precisely to avoid obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: The want of precise determination of ideas is the cause of no small obscurity and confusion in men’s thoughts and discourses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before arguing or enquiring, ensure key terms are clearly defined (i.e., the ideas they stand for are fixed). This is practical advice for clearer communication and dispute resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of inquiry (origins, extent, faith/opinion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-part method: (1) inquire into the original of ideas (how the understanding is furnished); (2) show what knowledge the understanding has by those ideas and the certainty/evidence/extent of it; (3) inquire into the nature and grounds of faith or opinion and examine reasons and degrees of assent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this ordered method when investigating human knowledge: start with origins of ideas, then the scope/limits of knowledge, then the basis of belief and assent. This provides a structured way to evaluate claims about knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay within the bounds of human understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Search out the bounds between opinion and knowledge; be cautious in meddling with things exceeding comprehension; stop when at the utmost extent of one’s tether and 'sit down in a quiet ignorance' of things beyond reach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for good inquiry: recognize limits of faculties, avoid overreaching. Practical implication: do not demand certainty where faculties only yield probability; avoid fruitless metaphysical speculation beyond cognitive capacities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept probability where certainty is unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not peremptorily or intemperately require demonstration and demand certainty where probability only is to be had, and which is sufficient to govern our concernments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practical reasoning, allow probabilistic judgment instead of insisting on unattainable certainty. Anti-pattern: dismissing useful beliefs because they lack absolute proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and use your cognitive capacities prudently
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of the powers of our minds helps determine what to undertake with hope of success and prevents both idle despair and universal doubt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposed inquiries or projects by whether they match the mind’s capacities; choose endeavours appropriate to one’s cognitive reach instead of attempting everything or nothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare and use 'idea' clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'idea' to stand for whatsoever is the object of the understanding when a man thinks — i.e., PHANTASM, NOTION, SPECIES, or whatever the mind can be employed about in thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state definitions of foundational terms (here, 'idea') at the outset so readers share the same basic vocabulary; this reduces equivocation and miscommunication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for acquisition of ideas before claiming innateness
rubrics_metrics.description: To show ideas or principles are not innate, demonstrate how by natural faculties men may attain all the knowledge they have without innate impressions; question claims of innate principles by examining experiential routes to agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation criterion for claims of innateness: require demonstration that universal assent cannot be produced by experience, memory, abstraction, or cultural transmission. Locke appeals to examples (children, idiots, savages) to test universality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate assent on first hearing is not proof of innateness
rubrics_metrics.description: General assent as soon as terms are understood is not a certain mark of innate principles; many acquired propositions (e.g., 'one and two are equal to three') are likewise assented to on first understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat ready assent upon understanding as evidence of native imprint; instead analyze whether the assent depends on pre-existing clear ideas or prior learning. Anti-pattern: inferring innateness solely from instantaneous assent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-evidence depends on clarity of ideas, not innate stamping
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-evidence of propositions arises from having clear and distinct ideas of what their terms mean, not because those propositions were originally imprinted on the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a proposition is self-evident, check whether the constituent ideas are distinct and understood. If so, the proposition will seem self-evident upon comprehension; this does not imply innateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological steps to knowledge (senses → memory → abstraction → language → reason)
rubrics_metrics.description: The senses first let in particular ideas and furnish the mind; memory lodges them; the mind abstracts and learns the use of general names; reason then uses these materials to deduce and extend knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this developmental account as a criterion for explanations of how knowledge is formed: prefer accounts that trace ideas to sensory input, retention, abstraction, and linguistic formulation before invoking purely innate sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate discovery by reason with innateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Reason is the faculty of deducing unknown truths from principles already known; if we need reason to discover a truth, that does not make the truth innate; claiming innateness because reason discovers it is circular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims of origin by asking whether purportedly innate truths require reasoning (hence prior known premises) for discovery. If so, they are better explained as discoveries from acquired premises rather than innate impressions.
